concept.name: Dollar bar
concept.definition: A dollar bar is an OHLCV bar built by aggregating trades until a fixed cumulative dollar value (price × quantity, e.g., $1,000,000) has traded. Sampling in money terms keeps bar information content comparable even as an instrument's price level changes over time.
concept.intuition: Each bar represents the same amount of cash changing hands, which keeps the sampling meaningful across years during which the share price may have multiplied.
concept.mechanics: Accumulate p_i·q_i over consecutive trades; when the running sum reaches the dollar threshold, emit an OHLCV bar and reset. López de Prado advocates dollar bars over share-volume bars because a fixed share count corresponds to very different economic significance as prices move, and suggests periodically adjusting the threshold for changes in free float or outstanding shares.
concept.failure_modes: The threshold must be maintained: corporate actions, price trends, and changing float can make a once-reasonable dollar threshold inappropriate, and implementations that cannot split block trades produce inexact bar values. Thresholds are not portable across instruments.
concept.misconceptions: Dollar bars are not just volume bars at a different scale — because they normalize by value, they remain economically comparable across price levels where share-volume bars do not.
concept.example: With $5M dollar bars on a large-cap stock, about 20 bars form on a $100M day, versus only 4 on a quiet $20M day.

citations.source: López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018)
